questions.question: Identify the hydrosphere: name its three states with locations, give the approximate proportions of salt, frozen and accessible fresh water, and distinguish the hydrosphere from the water cycle.
questions.expected_answer: The hydrosphere is all the Earth's water: liquid (oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater), ice (polar sheets, glaciers, icebergs, permafrost) and water vapour in the atmosphere. About 97 percent is salty ocean water; most of the fresh remainder is locked in ice; the accessible fresh liquid water is well under one percent of the total. The hydrosphere is the store of water; the water cycle is the set of processes (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, transpiration) that move water between stores — the hydrosphere is not itself a cycle.

questions.question: Explain how building a dam affects the lives of people and the ecology of a region, and name the investigation methods the syllabus recommends for studying this.
questions.expected_answer: Benefits: stores seasonal rain for reliable drinking water, irrigation and sometimes hydroelectric power (e.g. Vaal and Gariep dams). Costs: upstream flooding displaces communities and drowns farmland; downstream the flattened flow ends nutrient-spreading floods, the wall blocks fish migration, and trapped sediment starves floodplains while filling the reservoir; still water shifts the ecology (water plants, mosquitoes). Study methods: interview people who have lived in the area for many years, consult literature about the region, and compare river ecology above and below the dam. Good answers weigh benefits against costs for the specific place.

questions.question: Describe how you would test a water sample's quality and then purify it, stating what each purification stage removes and what survives.
questions.expected_answer: Test pH, then run the ion tests: nitric acid (fizzing = carbonate), then silver nitrate (white = chloride, cream = bromide, yellow = iodide), then barium nitrate (acid-fast white = sulphate); test strips read pH, nitrates and nitrites (contamination warnings), and a microscope checks for microorganisms. Purify by sedimentation (settles grit), filtration through sand/filter paper (traps fine particles), then disinfection with chlorine — or boiling — to kill microbes, which pass filters. Dissolved ions survive both filtering and boiling; removing them requires distillation/desalination.
